title: Minnesota lawyer suspended over fake AI case citations

reading.body:
An attorney submitted a legal memorandum to a Minnesota court containing fake case citations generated by an AI system. The two nonexistent cases, Anderson v. City of Biwabik and Doherty v. Alma E. Clark Memorial Home, were cited alongside a false quotation from a real case and additional citation errors. The attorney had used the AI system to research or draft portions of the filing without verifying the outputs against actual legal databases or case law.

The failure occurred in a court filing, where the opposing counsel discovered the fabricated citations and brought them to the judge's attention. This would have been caught by a human review of the memorandum against published case law before submission, or by verification of AI-generated citations against legal databases before relying on them in an official court document.

It is not established whether the attorney deliberately used unverified AI output or was unaware that the system had hallucinated the citations.

reports.title: Minnesota lawyer suspended over fake AI case citations

summary:
Minnesota attorney Faisal S. Ahmed was suspended for submitting fake legal citations generated by artificial intelligence in a 2025 court filing. Ahmed, who has been licensed since 2014, cited two nonexistent cases, Anderson v. City of Biwabik and Doherty v. Alma E. Clark Memorial Home, in a legal memorandum filed in Hennepin County Court. He also included a false quotation from a real case and two citation errors. The opposing attorney discovered these problems and brought them to Judge Lois Conroy's attention during an August hearing.

Conroy ruled against Ahmed's client, the owner of a Robbinsdale food store, ordering him to pay $233,563 in back rent to his landlord. She then fined Ahmed $5,000 and referred him to the Minnesota Lawyer's Professional Responsibility Board. According to state disciplinary filings, Ahmed agreed to a 30-day suspension of his law license and to pay an additional $900 in costs. This incident is part of a growing problem, with over 800 documented instances of AI-generated fake legal citations occurring in courts nationwide.
